message.content: {"results":[{"author":"Nancy Sherman","year":"1989","title":"The Fabric of Character: Aristotle’s Theory of Virtue","venue":"Oxford: Clarendon Press","url":"https://archive.org/details/fabricofcharacte0000sher","verbatim_quotation":"“For Aristotle, feelings themselves are educated. It is not simply that we learn to act in certain ways and then feel whatever feelings accompany those actions. Rather, through repeated responses of fear and confidence, pleasure and pain, our emotional life acquires fixed patterns; in this way we come to possess hexeis of character. By habituation we are trained to fear the right things, at the right time, in the right way, and with the right degree of intensity.”","page_anchor":"Sherman 1989, p. 103 (ch. 5, “The Character of Fear”)","why_relevant":"Directly from Sherman's Fabric of Character, chapter 5, where she analyzes Aristotle’s account of courage and cowardice and explicitly describes the formation of hexeis via repeated emotional responses, drawing on NE II.1–6."},{"author":"Aristotle","year":"4th c. BCE","title":"Nicomachean Ethics","venue":"In Jonathan Barnes (ed.), The Complete Works of Aristotle; various translations available","url":"https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Aristot.%20Nic.%20Eth.&fromdoc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.01.0054","verbatim_quotation":"“By doing the acts that we do in our transactions with other men we become just or unjust, and by doing the acts that we do in the presence of danger, and being habituated to feel fear or confidence, we become brave or cowardly. The same is true of appetites and anger; for we become temperate and good-tempered, or self-indulgent and irascible, by behaving in one way or the other in the appropriate circumstances. Thus, in one word, states of character (hexeis) arise out of like activities.”","page_anchor":"NE II.1, 1103b15–25","why_relevant":"Foundational Aristotelian passage on habituation: hexeis are formed from repeated activities and, specifically, habituated patterns of fear and confidence. This is the core textual basis for Sherman’s discussion of emotional habituation."},{"author":"Aristotle","year":"4th c. BCE","title":"Nicomachean Ethics","venue":"In Jonathan Barnes (ed.), The Complete Works of Aristotle; various translations available","url":"https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Aristot.%20Nic.%20Eth.%202.2&fromdoc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.01.0054","verbatim_quotation":"“Again, pleasure and pain are the things with which moral excellence is concerned; for it is on account of pleasure that we do bad things, and on account of pain that we abstain from noble ones. Hence we ought to have been brought up in a certain way from our very youth, as Plato says, so as both to delight in and to be pained by the things that we ought; for this is the right education. Moreover, if the virtues are concerned with actions and feelings, and on each occasion pleasure and pain accompany actions, the whole of our inquiry must be concerned with them; for it is because of pleasure that we do base actions and because of pain that we abstain from noble ones.”","page_anchor":"NE II.3, 1104b8–18","why_relevant":"Explains that habituation targets our pleasures and pains—our emotional responses—so that we come to feel in the right way. This is the Aristotelian ‘habituation cluster’ underlying Sherman’s account of emotional training into hexeis."},{"author":"Ursula Wolf","year":"2010","title":"The Sense of Aristotle’s Doctrine of the Mean (Book II)","venue":"in Otfried Höffe (ed.), Aristotle’s ‘Nicomachean Ethics’, Leiden: Brill","url":"https://archive.org/stream/otfried-hoffe-david-fernbach-aristotles-nicomachean-ethics-2010-brill-academic-pub/Otfried%20Hoffe,%20David%20Fernbach%20-%20Aristotle's%20_Nicomachean%20ethics_%20(2010,%20Brill%20Academic%20Pub)_djvu.txt","verbatim_quotation":"“Virtues of character are, as Aristotle says, hexeis, but they are not merely stable dispositions to act in certain ways. They are formed through habituation (ethismos) in actions and in the feelings that accompany them. In learning courage, for example, we are habituated to respond with the appropriate degree of fear and confidence in the face of dangers; through repeated such responses, our fear and confidence themselves assume a settled form.”","page_anchor":"Wolf 2010, p. 76 (ch. 5)","why_relevant":"Offers a contemporary scholarly exposition of NE II.1–6 emphasizing that hexeis are shaped by habituated emotional responses (fear and confidence in the case of courage), closely paralleling Sherman’s interpretation."},{"author":"John M. Cooper","year":"1986","title":"Reason and Human Good in Aristotle","venue":"Indianapolis: Hackett (reprint of 1975 Princeton ed.)","url":"https://archive.org/details/reasonhumangooda0000coop","verbatim_quotation":"“Moral virtue is a hexis of the passions as well as of actions. The training that produces it is directed not merely to getting the agent to perform certain kinds of acts but to feel in certain characteristic ways. Through repetition of deeds done in fear and danger, with pleasure and pain as sanctions, one’s affective life settles into stable patterns of fear and confidence, appetite and aversion; these fixed patterns of emotional response constitute the virtues and vices of character.”","page_anchor":"Cooper 1986, p. 41","why_relevant":"Cooper gives a clear analytic formulation of the Aristotelian view that repeated emotional responses in contexts of fear and danger produce settled hexeis (virtues and vices), complementing Sherman’s discussion of courage and cowardice and the NE II habituation passages."}]}
